summary: Builds the people, partnerships, funding and operating infrastructure King’s needs to create high-quality experiential opportunities, connect students and graduates with employers in the UK and internationally, widen access to purposeful global experience, remove barriers to participation, and support successful transition into graduate futures.
detailSummary:
King’s already holds extensive relationships with employers, industry, public bodies, community and third-sector organisations, civic and cultural partners, international organisations and alumni. It also has strong careers expertise, an established Global Mobility service, pockets of student-opportunity funding, philanthropic relationships and locally developed processes for experiential activity. These assets are distributed across faculties and professional services and are not yet consistently visible, coordinated or activated as one coherent institutional engine for opportunity and graduate success.

The proposition therefore brings together six connected capabilities. First, King’s will preserve and strengthen the common operating infrastructure through which experiential opportunities are sourced, designed, approved, promoted, delivered, supported and evaluated. This includes clearer roles across central teams and faculties; proportionate standards for quality, accessibility, safeguarding, risk, data and student support; common templates and agreements; simpler contracting and payment routes; better partner intelligence; and a clearer institutional opportunity pipeline. Delivery remains distributed: the infrastructure should make local delivery easier, safer and more consistent rather than centralising it.

Second, King’s will create dedicated domestic experiential opportunity-translation and partnership-infrastructure capacity from 2027/28 at the same planned staffing level as the fully developed international employer-engagement team. The Core planning assumption is £214,089 annualised, equivalent on the current fully loaded role-cost basis to 1 x G6 and 3 x G5. The exact domestic role titles and allocation should be informed by the first-year capability review and demand emerging through 2.1.4, 2.2.3 and 2.2.4, but the resource level is deliberately aligned with the international team. This capacity will turn UK employer, alumni, civic, cultural, community and other external relationships into well-formed student opportunities through brokerage, scoping, learning-design translation, contracting, partner onboarding, payments, administration and handover into near-curriculum and flexible opportunity routes.

Third, King’s will create dedicated international employer-engagement capacity, but phase the four-post team across the three delivery years rather than mobilising it immediately in full. In 2027/28, King’s will establish the G6 Employer Relations & Insights Manager (International) to protect existing international relationships, coordinate the portfolio and establish the operating model. In 2028/29, the G5 East Asia Adviser will be added to deepen the proven East Asia portfolio. In 2029/30, two further G5 Advisers will extend capacity across South and South East Asia and Europe and North America. A £50,000 annual non-pay envelope will support employer-facing and in-country activity from 2027/28. This capability is intended to improve access to relevant employers and labour-market intelligence for students and graduates while also strengthening King’s employability proposition in strategically important recruitment markets.

Fourth, King’s will strengthen Global Mobility with two incremental opportunity-development posts from September 2027: one G6 and one G5. These roles are intended to add growth and translation capacity rather than duplicate the existing service’s core exchange administration. Working with the established Global Mobility team, faculties and King’s Edge, they will grow and broker a broader mix of purposeful outward mobility, including shorter-form, experiential, work-related and other accessible international opportunities; connect mobility more deliberately to skills and graduate futures; and help turn overseas partnerships and propositions into student-ready opportunities that can feed the flexible and near-curriculum offer.

Fifth, King’s will establish a small Graduate Transitions function from September 2028, comprising a G7 Head of Graduate Transitions and a G6 Graduate Transitions Coach. Deferring mobilisation until the second cost year keeps the 2027/28 investment focused on opportunity generation and infrastructure while allowing the graduate-transition model, targeting logic and evidence base to be designed in advance. Once live, the function will move support beyond a predominantly reactive model by using Careers Readiness and other available data to identify graduates who may be at risk of poorer outcomes and provide targeted coaching, job-search support, employer referral and other interventions through the critical post-completion period captured by Graduate Outcomes.

Sixth, the deliverable will retain the existing access and opportunity-growth work. King’s will review and consolidate financial support for students undertaking employment-enhancing and developmental activity, with the intended direction of a coherent Student Opportunities Fund combining low-friction microbursaries of around £150-£250 with more substantial awards of around £4,000 for genuine out-of-pocket participation costs. Any new award pot sits outside the King’s Edge mobilisation ask and requires a separate institutional, consolidated-fund, philanthropic or other funding route. Alumni engagement and philanthropy will also be used deliberately to grow the supply of opportunity, including service-learning and social-good projects and models in which paid PhD project leads can mobilise flexible opportunities for wider student participation.

The causal logic is that King’s can create more meaningful and accessible experience, connect it more effectively to employers and graduate destinations, widen access to purposeful international experience, and improve institutional efficiency by joining up assets it already holds with targeted new capabilities. The fully mobilised Core resource proposition remains £714,058 annualised: £214,089 domestic experiential opportunity-translation staffing, £214,089 international employer-engagement staffing, £126,265 Graduate Transitions staffing, £109,615 Global Mobility opportunity-development staffing and a £50,000 international employer-engagement non-pay envelope. The investment is deliberately phased, giving an annualised Core run-rate of £431,082 in 2027/28, £609,584 in 2028/29 and £714,058 in 2029/30 once the full international team is in place. These figures are planning run-rates rather than a pro-rata payroll cashflow and should be converted into in-year budget requirements by Finance once exact start dates are agreed. All grade-based staffing figures are treated as fully loaded planning costs including employer National Insurance and pension/superannuation and should be validated with Finance/HR before approval.

caseForChange.problem: King’s has substantial external relationships, careers expertise, an established Global Mobility service, alumni connection and pockets of student-opportunity funding, but the infrastructure that turns these assets into opportunity and positive graduate destinations is fragmented. Relationship management, opportunity design, contracting, risk, payments, partner intelligence, international employer engagement, global opportunity development, graduate support and financial-access mechanisms can operate separately. Domestic external relationships are not always translated into student-ready experiential opportunities at the scale required, and the institution has limited incremental capacity to grow and translate a broader portfolio of purposeful outward mobility beyond existing core provision. This creates duplicated effort, missed connections, uneven access, fragile international employer capability and a reactive transition model for graduates who need additional support.
caseForChange.opportunity: King’s can create a stronger institutional engine that connects domestic experiential opportunity translation, shared operating infrastructure, employer relationships, international labour-market capability, global mobility opportunity development, proactive graduate transition, alumni engagement, philanthropy and student financial support. Shared standards can reduce friction and duplication without centralising delivery. A domestic team resourced at the same level as the fully developed international employer-engagement team can turn external interest into well-formed projects, placements, live briefs, challenges and other experiential routes at meaningful scale. Phasing the international team over three years protects affordability while allowing capability and evidence to build progressively. Incremental Global Mobility capacity can grow shorter-form and employability-linked international opportunities without displacing the existing team’s core exchange work. A small Graduate Transitions function can then be introduced from September 2028, once the first-year infrastructure is established, to target support where it is most needed. A coherent Student Opportunities Fund and philanthropic propositions can remove financial barriers and grow opportunity supply.
caseForChange.whyNow: King’s Edge is increasing the volume and ambition of experiential opportunity within and beyond the curriculum at the same time as the graduate labour market becomes more challenging and employability becomes more important to student choice. Growth through 2.1.4, 2.2.3 and 2.2.4 will create additional demand for domestic partner sourcing, brokerage and opportunity translation, including global opportunity as a thematic priority. Existing East Asia employability activity has demonstrated value but is unsupported by dedicated resource and has displaced domestic employer-engagement capacity. The existing Global Mobility team already facilitates study abroad and overseas traineeships, but Edge creates a case for additional opportunity-development capacity focused on growth, accessibility and stronger connection to graduate futures. Graduate support remains largely reactive after completion. A phased investment profile allows King’s to address these gaps without loading the full recurrent cost into the first delivery year.
caseForChange.intendedChange: King’s moves from fragmented relationship, opportunity, funding and graduate-transition activity towards connected employability and experiential infrastructure. Domestic external relationships are converted into student-ready opportunities through a dedicated team resourced at parity with the fully developed international employer-engagement function; staff and partners work through clearer routes and common processes; international employer capability grows in planned stages over the three delivery years; a broader range of students can access purposeful global experience; students have more consistent access to meaningful experience and financial support; and a proactive graduate-transition function is added from September 2028 once the core opportunity infrastructure is established. King’s can then evidence both Education and Student Success benefits and wider recruitment and reputation benefits from the same institutional capability.

problemSolved: King’s does not yet consistently convert its distributed external relationships, employability capability, global partnerships, alumni connection and opportunity funding into a coherent supply of accessible domestic and international experience and sustained support through the transition into graduate destinations.
whatChanges: King’s establishes connected domestic opportunity-translation, experiential, international employer-engagement, global mobility, access and graduate-transition infrastructure that can generate and sustain more opportunities, reduce operational friction, widen purposeful international experience, remove financial barriers and intervene proactively where graduates need additional support.
